answer: In unincorporated Miami-Dade and Hillsborough counties, a new in-ground home pool needs plans sealed by an architect or engineer.

Miami-Dade County’s pool permit page says the drawings must be signed and sealed by a design professional (architect or engineer). Hillsborough County’s residential pool checklist asks for building plans digitally signed and sealed by a State of Florida registered architect or engineer. Elsewhere in Florida, ask the building department that issues your permit what it requires. For a public pool, section 514.03, Florida Statutes, requires an application to the Department of Health for an operating permit before the building permit application. The department’s application instructions ask for the name and contact details of the engineer or design architect who stamped the plans.

sources.title: Miami-Dade County, How to Apply for a Permit
Florida Department of Health, DH4159 application instructions

answer: In Bellevue, yes: the city says a pool plan must be designed and stamped by a Washington State-licensed professional or structural engineer.

Clark County asks for engineering plans for in-ground pools stamped by an engineer or architect licensed in Washington. For private pools or spas in unincorporated King County, the county asks for construction drawings with engineering calculations or an approved ICC ES report. Elsewhere in Washington, ask the building department that issues your permit what it requires. For a pool covered by the state’s water recreation facility rules (chapter 246-260 of the Washington Administrative Code), WAC 246-260-021(1)(b) requires plans prepared, stamped and signed by an engineer or architect. That chapter does not apply to a pool used only by residents and invited guests at a single-family dwelling or a duplex owned by its residents.

sources.title: City of Bellevue, Pool and Spa Plan
King County, Private Swimming Pools or Spas
King County, Permits, inspections, and codes

answer: In Howard County, yes: all residential swimming pool plans must be signed and sealed by an engineer.

Howard County says so in its September 2025 memo and its pool checklist. Elsewhere in Maryland, ask the building department that issues your permit what it requires. For public pools and spas, COMAR 10.17.01.05 requires plans prepared by a licensed or certified professional engineer, architect, draftsman, or a person with extensive experience in the design of pools and spas.

sources.title: Howard County, residential swimming pool memo
Howard County, residential swimming pool checklist

answer: New Jersey’s construction code requires an architect’s or engineer’s seal on submitted plans, with a conditional exception for a single-family homeowner who prepared his or her own plans.

N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.15(f) calls for the seal and signature of the registered architect or licensed engineer who prepared the plans. The construction official waives the seal for that homeowner on conditions. They include that the plans are for a detached structure used only as the homeowner’s private residence, and that the homeowner submits an affidavit. Ask your construction office whether it applies that exception to a pool. Manalapan Township asks for signed and sealed plans for a residential in-ground pool. For public pools, N.J.A.C. 8:26-2.2 requires all documents to be sealed and certified by a licensed architect or professional engineer.

sources.title: Manalapan Township, Residential Pool Permit Application

answer: For public pool work costing $15,000 or more, yes: the plans must bear the seal of an engineer or architect licensed in Michigan.

Michigan rule R 325.2113 requires plans prepared by, and bearing the seal of, a professional engineer or architect licensed in Michigan when a new public pool and related facilities, or a modification of one, cost $15,000 or more. EGLE, the state environment department, says every new or modified public pool needs a construction permit. For a home pool, ask the building department that issues your permit what it requires.

In Pittsburgh, the city’s Residential Pool Form requires drawings prepared by a Pennsylvania-licensed architect or engineer for a custom-built pool or spa, or for an in-ground pool deeper than 4 feet.

Philadelphia’s EZ Permit Standard lets pools and spas at an existing one-family home be permitted without submitting plans if they meet its conditions and design limits. Elsewhere in Pennsylvania, ask the building department that issues your permit what it requires. For a public bathing place, 28 Pa. Code § 18.12 requires permit drawings prepared by or under the supervision of a registered professional engineer or registered architect. Each drawing must bear that engineer’s or architect’s seal.

sources.title: City of Pittsburgh, Residential Pool Form
City of Philadelphia, EZ Permit Standard for pools and spas

answer: For a public pool, a Tennessee rule requires the pool’s designer, architect or engineer to certify its structural stability and safety.

Under Department of Health Rule 1200-23-05-.03(2)(c), the certification goes in the plans and specifications submitted. The rule’s public pool definition excludes residential pools, meaning pools that serve no more than three living units and are used only by those families and their private guests. The rule lists pools at apartments, condominiums and subdivisions as public pools. The City of Knoxville lists public pools among Assembly occupancies (gathering places with a calculated occupant load of 50 or more) and says a registered design professional must prepare the plans for that occupancy. For a home pool, ask the building department that issues your permit what it requires.

sources.title: Tennessee Department of Health, Rule Chapter 1200-23-05
City of Knoxville, Fast Fact Guides

answer: For an in-ground home pool, it depends on state law and local rules.

Oregon’s 2026 Residential Specialty Code exempts in-ground pools at one- and two-family homes from building permits unless a municipality’s ordinance requires one. Fences serving as a pool barrier still need a building permit statewide. When you apply for a permit, the code says construction documents must be prepared by a registered design professional where ORS chapters 671 and 672 require it. Medford’s pool guidelines say a pool must be engineered if it does not meet the proper setbacks from a foundation. Ask your city or county building department what it requires. For public pools, Oregon Health Authority rule OAR 333-060-1000, section 4.1.1.4, requires plans prepared by a registered or licensed design professional.

sources.title: City of Medford, Swimming Pool Submittal Guidelines

answer: In Chandler, yes, for custom in-ground pools and spas: the city requires pool engineering plans stamped and sealed by an engineer.

Mesa’s residential construction page lists “architectural, structural, and engineer sealed drawings” for swimming pools. Pima County’s custom pool submittal requirements list sealed structural calculations among the items required when applicable to the project. Elsewhere in Arizona, ask the building department that issues your permit what it requires. Maricopa County reviews plans for public and semi-public pools. It says they must be prepared by, or under the supervision of, a registered Arizona professional engineer or architect, or a swimming pool contractor with an A-9, A-19, KA-5 or KA-6 license.

sources.title: City of Chandler, Home Owners Building Permit Manual
Maricopa County, Swimming Pools Management: Projects
